md: ## Upside down over the Pacific A few seconds before 1620 on January 31, 2000, an Alaska Airlines MD-83 was flying upside down above the ocean off southern California. The flight data recorder showed that its nose had dropped to 70 degrees below the horizon and that it had rolled until it was inverted. In the cockpit, the captain kept working the problem. "push and roll, push and roll," he said. Then, "ok, we are inverted…and now we gotta get it." Later still, "gotta get it over again…at least upside down we're flyin." Less than 20 seconds after that last remark, the recordings stopped. Flight 261 struck the Pacific about 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island. All 88 people on board died. They were 2 pilots, 3 cabin crew members and 83 passengers, among them 3 children under 2 years old who were held on a lap. By then the pilots had been fighting one failing part for about two and a half hours. It sat at the top of the tail, out of sight, and it had been wearing away for years. ## A routine flight home Flight 261 was a scheduled flight from Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, to Seattle, with a stop planned in San Francisco. The pilots who brought the airplane in that day described the crew as rested, relaxed and in good spirits. The captain, 53, had about 17,750 flight hours. The first officer, 57, had about 8,140, nearly all of them in the MD-80. To follow what went wrong, it helps to know how this airplane controls its pitch, meaning whether the nose points up or down. The MD-80 has a T-tail. The horizontal stabilizer, the small wing at the back, sits on top of the vertical fin. For finer, longer-lasting adjustment, called trim, the whole stabilizer tilts. Its front edge is raised and lowered by a jackscrew assembly, a vertical screw that turns through a fixed nut, much like a car jack. The screw is the acme screw, and the nut, made of softer aluminum bronze, is the acme nut. Two electric motors turn the screw, a faster primary motor and a slower alternate one that the autopilot uses. Everything depends on the threads inside that nut. The report states that the designers assumed at least one set of threads would always be intact and engaged. No other structure in the airplane does the jackscrew's job. ## A stabilizer that would not move All times here are Pacific standard time on a 24-hour clock. The airplane took off about 1337, and during the first part of the climb the stabilizer moved normally. At 1349, passing about 23,400 feet, it moved for the last time. It would not move again for 2 hours and 20 minutes. At 1353 the autopilot disconnected, most likely by the crew after a warning light showed the airplane was out of trim. From then on the pilots flew by hand, at first with up to 50 pounds of pull on the control columns, easing to about 10 pounds as the airplane sped up and burned fuel at 31,050 feet. The captain later said they had tried just about every combination of switches and handles to move the stabilizer. At 1546 the autopilot went back on. The cockpit voice recorder (CVR) kept only the last 31 minutes, starting at 1549. By then the crew was already talking with company dispatch and maintenance in Seattle about a jammed stabilizer and a possible diversion to Los Angeles. The dispatcher pointed out that landing in Los Angeles would mean a delay of an hour to an hour and a half because of heavy traffic. The captain answered, "I really didn't want to hear about the flow being the reason you're calling us cause I'm concerned about overflying suitable airports." He settled on Los Angeles because it offered a dry runway with little crosswind, which meant a lower speed over the ground on landing. Just before 1608 a company mechanic in Los Angeles came on the radio and asked whether they had tried the "suitcase handles and the pickle switches," slang for the trim handles on the center console and the trim switches on the control wheels. "yea we tried everything together," the captain said. He described an electrical load meter that spiked when they used the primary motor, which told him "the motor's tryin to run but the brake won't move it." With the alternate motor, he said, "nothing happens." ## The first dive At 1609, after more talk with the mechanic, the captain told the first officer he was taking the autopilot off. The investigation concluded that he did this while activating the primary trim system again. The recorder picked up a clunk, then two faint thumps. Within 3 to 4 seconds the stabilizer swung to a nose-down position beyond anything the flight data recorder could register, and the airplane pitched over. "it got worse," the captain said. To air traffic control he radioed, "center Alaska two sixty one we are uh in a dive here," and added, "I've lost control, vertical pitch." The overspeed warning sounded for 33 seconds. In about 80 seconds the airplane fell from about 31,050 feet to between 23,000 and 24,000 feet, reaching 353 knots. With the speedbrakes out and an estimated 130 to 140 pounds of pull on the controls, the pilots stopped the dive. "whatever we did is no good, don't do that again," the first officer said. The captain agreed. "it went down it went to full nose down." The first officer told the next controller, "we have a jammed stabilizer and we're maintaining altitude with difficulty." For the next several minutes they held the airplane level with about 120 pounds of pull. ## The final minutes The captain asked to descend and change the airplane's configuration "out here over the bay," to make sure he could control it before an approach. At 1617 the first officer made what would be the last radio call. The captain told a flight attendant to get everyone strapped in. The flight attendant reported, "ok we had like a big bang back there." The captain answered, "yea I heard it," and soon added, "I think the stab trim thing is broke." Near 18,000 feet the captain had the slats and then 11 degrees of flap extended. Slats and flaps are wing panels that add lift at lower speeds. "its pretty stable right here," he said, though he wanted to slow to 180 knots. Nine seconds later he ordered them retracted, and the recording does not show why. He then described a plan that the NTSB read as another try at the trim with the load taken off the tail. The first officer pushed back. "I think if it's controllable, we oughta just try to land it." The captain agreed. "ok lets head for LA." About five seconds later the recorder picked up a series of thumps. "you feel that?" the first officer asked. The captain called for the slats again. At 1619 and 36 seconds the CVR recorded an "extremely loud noise." The nose dropped at nearly 25 degrees per second, and the load factor fell to minus 3 G, well past the point where loose objects float. Within seconds the airplane was pointing 70 degrees down and rolling left, and soon it was on its back. For more than a minute the pilots kept trying. "push push push…push the blue side up." The captain called for left rudder, then right rudder. At 1620 and 56 seconds the captain said, "ah here we go." The recordings ended a moment later. ## What the sea gave back The wreckage lay about 700 feet down, spread over a quarter mile of ocean floor. Through mid-March 2000, teams used sonar, remotely operated vehicles and finally a trawler dragging the bottom, and raised about 85 percent of the fuselage. The key piece came up still attached to the stabilizer's front spar. Wrapped around the acme screw were thin metal coils. They were the threads of the acme nut, sheared out of it. The nut itself was found in the tail wreckage with a nearly smooth bore and only small ridges where its threads had been. Investigators calculated that about 90 percent of the thread thickness had worn away before the rest sheared off. A nut at the maximum wear allowed in service would have lost only about 22 percent. There was no grease, fresh or old, on the working part of the screw or inside the nut. The small passage through which the nut is greased held a dry, black, claylike residue. Tests showed that seawater does not significantly remove grease, and other parts of this airplane still carried visible grease after 7 and a half days underwater. The evidence told a two-stage story. As the airplane climbed through 23,400 feet, the last worn threads gave way and the screw jammed in the stripped nut. When the primary motor ran again at 1609, the jam broke, and air loads pulled the screw up through the nut until a stop at the bottom of the screw caught against the nut's underside. That held for about 10 minutes. Meanwhile the heavy, uneven loads cracked the torque tube, a titanium tube running through the screw, by low-cycle fatigue, meaning failure after relatively few cycles of high stress. When it broke, the stabilizer bore on fairing brackets atop the fin that were never meant to carry it. The loud noise was most likely those brackets failing. The stabilizer's front edge then swung far upward, forcing the nose down in a dive from which recovery was not possible. ## How the threads wore away The nut had worn at about 0.012 inch per 1,000 flight hours, roughly 12 times the expected rate. The NTSB ruled out the type of grease, the screw's surface finish, abrasive debris and abnormal loads. What remained was lack of lubrication. The last recorded greasing was done in September 1999 at Alaska's San Francisco base. The mechanic responsible said the job took about an hour. Boeing indicated that, done properly, it takes more than 4 person-hours. About 40 percent of the other fittings on the same task card were found dry or semi-dry. The wear was too great to have built up in the four months since, so the NTSB concluded that more than one lubrication had likely been missed or done poorly. The margin around those greasings had also shrunk. In 1987 Alaska lubricated the jackscrew every 500 flight hours. Through a series of extensions approved by the FAA, the last one based on the manufacturer's own longer recommendation, that became 8 months in 1996, about 2,550 flight hours, with no flight-hour cap. The longer the interval, the longer a single missed greasing leaves the parts dry. The check meant to catch wear had been stretched as well. Wear is measured with an end play check, which gauges how far the screw can shift inside the nut. Alaska tied it to every other heavy maintenance check and kept lengthening those checks, so the interval grew to 30 months, about 9,550 flight hours, far beyond the 7,000 or 7,200 hours the manufacturer recommended. This airplane's last end play check, in September 1997 in Oakland, measured 0.040 inch, exactly the limit. A mechanic who had worked on every one of the airline's MD-80s said he had never seen a jackscrew worn that much. A work card was written to replace the nut. Then a lead mechanic ordered a recheck, which measured 0.033 inch five times, and the airplane went back into service. No new jackscrew was ever ordered. The NTSB noted that either reading permitted a return to service. It also found that the restraining fixture Alaska had made in-house for the check did not meet Boeing's specifications and could read low, though it could not determine whether that affected this measurement. The airplane flew nearly 9,000 more hours before the threads failed. Had Alaska followed the manufacturer's flight-hour interval, the assembly would have been checked 1,800 to 2,000 hours before the accident. The NTSB found the probable cause to be "a loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's acme nut threads," caused by excessive wear "resulting from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly." It named three contributing factors. The first was Alaska's extended lubrication interval and the FAA's approval of it. The second was Alaska's extended end play check interval and the FAA's approval of it. The third was the absence on the MD-80 of a fail-safe mechanism to prevent the catastrophic effects of total acme nut thread loss. The screw and nut each had two thread spirals, yet both wear together, so they gave no backup against wear. The board also weighed the crew's actions. It called the decision not to turn back to Puerto Vallarta understandable, given that no checklist required landing as soon as possible, and the diversion to Los Angeles prudent and appropriate. It found that dispatch appeared to have tried to steer the crew toward San Francisco. It judged flying on autopilot with a jammed stabilizer inappropriate and said the repeated trim attempts went well beyond the checklist. It could not determine how much those attempts contributed, and it noted that the failure exceeded anything the crew had been trained to expect. Beyond the cockpit, it found widespread systemic deficiencies in Alaska's maintenance program and FAA surveillance of the airline that had been deficient for at least several years. ## What changed Eleven days after the crash, the FAA issued an airworthiness directive, a binding safety order, requiring jackscrew inspections across the DC-9, MD-80, MD-90 and 717 fleets, lubrication every 650 flight hours and end play checks every 2,000 flight hours. A later directive kept those limits and required operators to report their end play results. The final report, adopted in December 2002, made 16 more recommendations to the FAA. Pilots with a failed flight control on an airplane that still flies should complete only the checklist and, if that fails, land at the nearest suitable airport. Dispatchers should not urge continued flight for the schedule's sake. Old grease should be cleaned off before new is applied, and each jackscrew lubrication should need an inspector's signoff. Extending critical maintenance intervals should require engineering data. The jackscrew should get a fail-safe design if practicable, and future stabilizer trim systems should not be certified with a single failure that can bring down the airplane. ## What remains Board member John Goglia, in a separate statement, called this "a maintenance accident, perhaps more purely so than any others we have seen," and stressed that the jackscrew is robust when it is cared for. The report as a whole also presses for a design that does not depend on grease alone. For pilots, the lesson is practical. When a flight control fails and the airplane still flies, run the checklist, stop experimenting, and head for the nearest suitable runway. For everyone else, the story turns on a can of grease, a measuring tool and a few signatures. A job that needed four careful hours was done in one, and each stretched interval looked reasonable on paper. Together they removed every chance to catch the wear before the airplane's last flight. ## Facts - **Date** January 31, 2000, about 1621 Pacific standard time - **Flight** Alaska Airlines flight 261, scheduled international passenger flight - **Aircraft** McDonnell Douglas MD-83, registration N963AS - **Route** Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, to Seattle, Washington, with a planned stop in San Francisco, California; diverting to Los Angeles at the time of the accident - **Location** Pacific Ocean, about 2.7 miles north of Anacapa Island, California - **People on board** 88 (2 pilots, 3 cabin crew members, 83 passengers) - **Fatalities** 88 - **Probable cause** Loss of airplane pitch control resulting from the in-flight failure of the horizontal stabilizer trim system jackscrew assembly's acme nut threads, caused by excessive wear resulting from Alaska Airlines' insufficient lubrication of the jackscrew assembly.
